---
title: "Turning on a Light in the Dark"
unit: 3
cluster: "Reading Sensors"
---

Many circuits need to know how much light there is, such as a night light or
a street lamp that turns itself on at dusk. A **light sensor** measures this,
and ours is an **LDR module**: a small board that gives both the light level
and whether it is darker than a level we set.

In this chapter, we'll learn how to:

- connect an LDR module to the board
- read whether it is dark, from its digital output
- set how dark is dark, with the screw on the module
- read the light level itself, from its analog output
- turn on the LED only when it is dark

## The LDR module

An **LDR**, or light-dependent resistor, is the round part with a squiggly
line on its face, at the end of the module. Its resistance changes with
light: low in bright light, and high in the dark. The module turns that into
a voltage between 0 and 3.3 volts, the same way the pot did.

A chip on the module compares that voltage with a level, set by the screw on
the blue **trimmer**, and turns a second output on or off. So the module has
two outputs, and four pins:

| Pin | Connects to   | What it does |
|-----|---------------|--------------|
| VCC | 3V3           | powers the module |
| GND | GND           | completes the circuit |
| DO  | a GPIO input  | digital output: 1 when it is darker than the level, 0 when it is brighter |
| AO  | an ADC pin    | analog output: a voltage that goes up as it gets darker |

The module also has two small LEDs. One lights while the module has power.
The other lights while DO is 0, that is, while it is brighter than the
level.

## Connecting the module

The module's pins stick straight out of one end, so it stands upright in the
breadboard, with the LDR at the top. Seen from the back, the pins are VCC,
GND, DO and AO, from left to right.

Start with the circuit that blinks an LED from D15, on the full-length
breadboard. Unplug the USB cable. Then:

1. Push the module's pins into `j32` to `j35`, with its back towards you:
   VCC in `j32`, GND in `j33`, DO in `j34` and AO in `j35`.
2. Connect `f32` to the bottom `+` rail with a red jumper wire. This gives
   VCC 3.3 volts.
3. Connect `f33` to the bottom `−` rail with a black jumper wire. This
   connects GND to GND.
4. Connect `i34` to `j9`, above D7, with a jumper wire. This connects DO to
   GPIO7.
5. Connect `h35` to `j11`, above A0, with a jumper wire. This connects AO to
   GPIO0, which has the ADC.

![The LED circuit from D15, on a full-length breadboard, with an LDR module standing in `j32` to `j35`, its back to us. Its VCC and GND connect to the bottom `+` and `−` rails, its DO to D7, and its AO to A0. Board photo: PCBCupid.](../images/glyph-c6-breadboard-ldr.svg)

Plug in the USB cable. The power LED on the module lights.

## Reading whether it is dark

Connect Thonny to the board, and set up GPIO7 as an input in the REPL:

```session
>>> from machine import ADC, Pin
```

```session
>>> dark = Pin(7, Pin.IN)
```

This time there is no `Pin.PULL_UP`. A push button only connects the pin to
GND, and leaves it floating when released. The module sets DO to 0 or to 3.3
volts itself, so the pin never floats.

Read the pin in the light of the room:

```session
>>> dark.value()
```

It returns 0: it is brighter than the level. Now cover the LDR with a
finger, and read the pin again:

```session
>>> dark.value()
```

This time it returns 1. As DO changes, the second LED on the module goes off
and on, so we can see the answer without reading the pin.

If the value does not change, or is 1 even in the light, the level is set
too far one way or the other. The next section sets it.

## Setting the level

The level is set on the module, not in the program. Turn the screw on the
blue trimmer with a small screwdriver, and watch the module's second LED:

1. With the LDR in the light of the room, turn the screw until the LED goes
   off.
2. Turn it back, slowly, until the LED just comes on again.

The module now switches when the light falls a little below the light of the
room. Cover the LDR with a finger, and the LED goes off. To make it switch
only when it is darker, turn the screw a little further back.

## Reading the light level

DO tells us only which side of the level the light is on. AO gives the
voltage itself, so the program can see how bright or dark it is. We read it
through the ADC, as we read the knob. Set up GPIO0 as an analog input:

```session
>>> light = ADC(Pin(0))
```

Read it in the light of the room:

```session
>>> light.read_u16()
```

`read_u16()` returns a number from 0 to 65535, as it did for the knob. Cover
the LDR with a finger, and read it again:

```session
>>> light.read_u16()
```

The number is now higher: the darker it is, the higher the voltage on AO.
Try it with the LDR under a hand, near a window, and with a phone's torch
shining on it, and watch the number change.

DO is AO compared with the level. Turning the screw does not change AO at
all; it only changes the voltage at which DO switches.

## Turning on the light in the dark

The program reads DO over and over, and turns the LED on while it reads 1.
Type this program in the editor:

```python
from machine import Pin

led = Pin(15, Pin.OUT)
dark = Pin(7, Pin.IN)

while True:
    if dark.value() == 1:
        led.on()
    else:
        led.off()
```

This is the program that lit the LED with the push button, with the module
in place of the button, and `== 1` in place of `== 0`, because DO is 1 in
the dark.

Click Run. In the light, the LED is off. Cover the LDR with your hand, and
the LED lights; take your hand away, and it goes off. Click Stop to end the
program.

::: {.callout-note}
When the light is close to the level, DO can switch on and off many times a
second, and the LED flickers. Move the module into more light or less, or
turn the screw a little.
:::

## Summary

A light sensor module gives the light level on AO, read through the ADC, and
whether it is darker than a level we set with a screw on DO, read like a
push button.

| Connection or code | What it does |
|--------------------|--------------|
| LDR | a resistor whose resistance is high in the dark and low in the light |
| VCC → 3V3, GND → GND | powers the module |
| DO → D7 | lets the program read whether it is darker than the level |
| AO → A0 | lets the program read the light level |
| Trimmer on the module | sets the level at which DO switches; does not change AO |
| `dark = Pin(7, Pin.IN)` | sets up GPIO7 as an input; no pull-up, since the module sets DO itself |
| `dark.value()` | returns 1 when it is darker than the level, and 0 when it is brighter |
| `light = ADC(Pin(0))` | sets up GPIO0 to measure the voltage on AO |
| `light.read_u16()` | returns the light level as a number from 0 to 65535; higher means darker |
| `if dark.value() == 1:` | is true while it is dark |
